| <a id="III.N3.1.3"></a>**III.N3.1.3** | But the passage from Brehm's Life of Animals, which is sometimes referred to, can hardly be taken as very conclusive. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N3.1.4"></a>**III.N3.1.4** | It occurs in his general description of monkeys; but his more detailed descriptions of separate species either contradict it or do not confirm it. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N3.1.5"></a>**III.N3.1.5** | Even as regards the cercopitheques, Brehm is affirmative in saying that they "nearly always live in bands, and very seldom in families" (French edition, p. 59). |  |  |
| <a id="III.N3.1.6"></a>**III.N3.1.6** | As to other species, the very numbers of their bands, always containing many males, render the "polygamous family" more than doubtful further observation is evidently wanted. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N4.1.1"></a>**III.N4.1.1** | Lubbock, Prehistoric Times, fifth edition, 1890. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N5.1.1"></a>**III.N5.1.1** | That extension of the ice-cap is admitted by most of the geologists who have specially studied the glacial age. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N5.1.2"></a>**III.N5.1.2** | The Russian Geological Survey already has taken this view as regards Russia, and most German specialists maintain it as regards Germany. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N5.1.3"></a>**III.N5.1.3** | The glaciation of most of the central plateau of France will not fail to be recognized by the French geologists, when they pay more attention to the glacial deposits altogether. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N6.1.1"></a>**III.N6.1.1** | Prehistoric Times, pp. 232 and 242. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.1"></a>**III.N7.1.1** | Bachofen, Das Mutterrecht, Stuttgart, 1861; Lewis H. Morgan, Ancient Society, or Researches in the Lines of Human Progress from Savagery through Barbarism to Civilization, New York, 1877; J.F. MacLennan, Studies in Ancient History, 1st series, new edition, 1886; 2nd series, 1896; L. Fison and A.W. Howitt, Kamilaroi and Kurnai, Melbourne. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.2"></a>**III.N7.1.2** | These four writers--as has been very truly remarked by Giraud Teulon,--starting from different facts and different general ideas, and following different methods, have come to the same conclusion. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.3"></a>**III.N7.1.3** | To Bachofen we owe the notion of the maternal family and the maternal succession; to Morgan--the system of kinship, Malayan and Turanian, and a highly gifted sketch of the main phases of human evolution; to MacLennan--the law of exogeny; and to Fison and Howitt--the cuadro, or scheme, of the conjugal societies in Australia. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.4"></a>**III.N7.1.4** | All four end in establishing the same fact of the tribal origin of the family. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.5"></a>**III.N7.1.5** | When Bachofen first drew attention to the maternal family, in his epoch-making work, and Morgan described the clan-organization,--both concurring to the almost general extension of these forms and maintaining that the marriage laws lie at the very basis of the consecutive steps of human evolution, they were accused of exaggeration. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.6"></a>**III.N7.1.6** | However, the most careful researches prosecuted since, by a phalanx of students of ancient law, have proved that all races of mankind bear traces of having passed through similar stages of development of marriage laws, such as we now see in force among certain savages. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N7.1.7"></a>**III.N7.1.7** | See the works of Post, Dargun, Kovalevsky, Lubbock, and their numerous followers: Lippert, Mucke, etc. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N8.1.1"></a>**III.N8.1.1** ⚑ | None |  |  |
| <a id="III.N9.1.1"></a>**III.N9.1.1** | For the Semites and the Aryans, see especially Prof. Maxim Kovalevsky's Primitive Law (in Russian), Moscow, 1886 and 1887. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N9.1.2"></a>**III.N9.1.2** | Also his Lectures delivered at Stockholm (Tableau des origines et de l'evolution de la famille et de la propriete, Stockholm, 1890), which represents an admirable review of the whole question. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N9.1.3"></a>**III.N9.1.3** | Cf. also A. Post, Die Geschlechtsgenossenschaft der Urzeit, Oldenburg 1875. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.1"></a>**III.N10.1.1** | It would be impossible to enter here into a discussion of the origin of the marriage restrictions. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.2"></a>**III.N10.1.2** | Let me only remark that a division into groups, similar to Morgan's Hawaian, exists among birds; the young broods live together separately from their parents. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.3"></a>**III.N10.1.3** | A like division might probably be traced among some mammals as well. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.4"></a>**III.N10.1.4** | As to the prohibition of relations between brothers and sisters, it is more likely to have arisen, not from speculations about the bad effects of consanguinity, which speculations really do not seem probable, but to avoid the too-easy precocity of like marriages. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.5"></a>**III.N10.1.5** | Under close cohabitation it must have become of imperious necessity. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.6"></a>**III.N10.1.6** | I must also remark that in discussing the origin of new customs altogether, we must keep in mind that the savages, like us, have their "thinkers" and savants-wizards, doctors, prophets, etc.--whose knowledge and ideas are in advance upon those of the masses. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N10.1.7"></a>**III.N10.1.7** | United as they are in their secret unions (another almost universal feature) they are certainly capable of exercising a powerful influence, and of enforcing customs the utility of which may not yet be recognized by the majority of the tribe. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N11.1.1"></a>**III.N11.1.1** | Col. Collins, in Philips' Researches in South Africa, London, 1828. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N11.1.2"></a>**III.N11.1.2** | Quoted by Waitz, ii. 334. |  |  |

| <a id="III.N28.1.2"></a>**III.N28.1.2** | Europeans, grown in the respect of Roman law, are seldom capable of understanding that force of tribal authority. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N28.1.3"></a>**III.N28.1.3** | "In fact," Dr. Rink writes, "it is not the exception, but the rule, that white men who have stayed for ten or twenty years among the Eskimo, return without any real addition to their knowledge of the traditional ideas upon which their social state is based. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N28.1.4"></a>**III.N28.1.4** | The white man, whether a missionary or a trader, is firm in his dogmatic opinion that the most vulgar European is better than the most distinguished native."--The Eskimo Tribes, p. 31. |  |  |

| <a id="III.N33.1.1"></a>**III.N33.1.1** | It is most remarkable that several writers (Middendorff, Schrenk, O. Finsch) described the Ostyaks and Samoyedes in almost the same words. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.2"></a>**III.N33.1.2** | Even when drunken, their quarrels are insignificant. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.3"></a>**III.N33.1.3** | "For a hundred years one single murder has been committed in the tundra;" "their children never fight;" "anything may be left for years in the tundra, even food and gin, and nobody will touch it;" and so on. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.4"></a>**III.N33.1.4** | Gilbert Sproat "never witnessed a fight between two sober natives" of the Aht Indians of Vancouver Island. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.5"></a>**III.N33.1.5** | "Quarrelling is also rare among their children." |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.6"></a>**III.N33.1.6** | (Rink, loc. cit.) |  |  |
| <a id="III.N33.1.7"></a>**III.N33.1.7** | And so on. |  |  |

| <a id="III.N39.1.1"></a>**III.N39.1.1** | It is remarkable, however, that in case of a sentence of death, nobody will take upon himself to be the executioner. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.2"></a>**III.N39.1.2** | Every one throws his stone, or gives his blow with the hatchet, carefully avoiding to give a mortal blow. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.3"></a>**III.N39.1.3** | At a later epoch, the priest will stab the victim with a sacred knife. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.4"></a>**III.N39.1.4** | Still later, it will be the king, until civilization invents the hired hangman. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.5"></a>**III.N39.1.5** | See Bastian's deep remarks upon this subject in Der Mensch in der Geschichte, iii. |  |  |

| <a id="III.N39.1.7"></a>**III.N39.1.7** | A remainder of this tribal habit, I am told by Professor E. Nys, has survived in military executions till our own times. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.8"></a>**III.N39.1.8** | In the middle portion of the nineteenth century it was the habit to load the rifles of the twelve soldiers called out for shooting the condemned victim, with eleven ball-cartridges and one blank cartridge. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N39.1.9"></a>**III.N39.1.9** | As the soldiers never knew who of them had the latter, each one could console his disturbed conscience by thinking that he was not one of the murderers. |  |  |
| <a id="III.N40.1.1"></a>**III.N40.1.1** | In Africa, and elsewhere too, it is a widely-spread habit, that if a theft has been committed, the next clan has to restore the equivalent of the stolen thing, and then look itself for the thief. |  |  |
